criteria_results.title: Argument responding to Defendant's Argument (D): SOX standing/publicly traded company issue

criteria_results.title: Conclusion requesting denial of the motion
criteria_results.reasoning: The memorandum’s conclusion expressly states that Plaintiff requests the Court deny Defendant’s motion for summary judgment on Counts I, II, and III, and the introduction also says the motion should be denied on all three claims. This is a request for denial in its entirety.

criteria_results.title: ISSUE_001: Hargrove-Caldwell email identified as key evidence of retaliatory motive
criteria_results.reasoning: The memorandum prominently cites the August 1, 2023 Hargrove-Caldwell email multiple times, quoting that Vasquez was the “obvious candidate,” that the Bank needed to “identify the source and contain this,” and Caldwell’s response, “Let me handle this.” It uses the email as direct evidence of knowledge, source-hunting, retaliatory motive, causation, and pretext.

criteria_results.title: ISSUE_001: Email defeats Defendant's argument that bank lacked knowledge
criteria_results.reasoning: The memorandum directly uses the Hargrove-Caldwell email to rebut the bank's claimed lack of knowledge of the FinCEN/OCC source, emphasizing that Hargrove identified Vasquez as the likely source, Caldwell said he would handle it, and that decisionmakers' belief or suspicion that she reported externally is sufficient to support retaliation under a perceived-whistleblower theory.

criteria_results.title: ISSUE_001: 13-day gap between email and PIP is highlighted
criteria_results.reasoning: The memorandum states that on August 14 Caldwell placed Vasquez on a PIP 13 days after the August 1 Hargrove-Caldwell email, and it uses that timing/proximity as evidence supporting retaliatory motive and causation.

criteria_results.title: ISSUE_002: Loan file deficiency rebutted with Internal Audit report
criteria_results.reasoning: The memorandum explicitly argues that the PIP's cited deficiencies in the Thornburg, Westlake, and Meridian loan files are contradicted by the May 15 Q1 2023 Internal Audit report, which rated those accounts satisfactory or better and recommended no corrective action.

criteria_results.title: ISSUE_002: Client complaint deficiency rebutted — Orion Gateway complaint
criteria_results.reasoning: The memorandum explicitly states that one client complaint came from Raymond Sellars, Orion Gateway's principal, and identifies Orion Gateway as the customer/entity whose suspicious activity Vasquez had reported. It uses that connection to argue the complaint's circumstances support a jury issue and pretext.

criteria_results.title: ISSUE_002: Client complaint deficiency rebutted — Thornburg declaration
criteria_results.reasoning: The memorandum explicitly cites the Thornburg Declaration multiple times for the proposition that Jeffrey Thornburg never complained about Vasquez's responsiveness and found her responsive, contradicting the PIP's client-complaint deficiency. See Material Fact 8 and Argument section III.A.3.

criteria_results.title: ISSUE_002: Origination target deficiency rebutted — $10M vs. $15M
criteria_results.reasoning: The memorandum expressly rebuts the origination-target PIP deficiency by stating that the signed 2023 Business Plan set Vasquez's Q2 target at $10 million, the PIP retroactively used $15 million, and Vasquez originated $11.3 million, exceeding the real written target.

criteria_results.title: ISSUE_002: Pretext framework applied to PIP deficiencies
criteria_results.reasoning: The memorandum expressly invokes a burden-shifting/retaliation framework, notes McDonnell Douglas as an alternative, and uses the contradicted PIP deficiencies—retroactive sales target, audit conflicts, allegedly false client complaints, and policy deviations—as evidence that the bank’s stated performance reasons were pretextual.

criteria_results.title: ISSUE_003: PIP duration of 32 days identified as violating bank policy
criteria_results.reasoning: The memorandum expressly states that the PIP ran only 32 days, cites Handbook § 7.4.3 / §§ 7.4.2–7.4.6, and states the policy requires a 60-to-90-day PIP period absent documented extraordinary circumstances. It also identifies the PIP as issued on August 14. Thus the required 32-day duration, 60–90 day policy requirement, and Section 7.4 citation are present.

criteria_results.title: ISSUE_003: Compressed PIP timeline argued as evidence of pretext
criteria_results.reasoning: The memorandum expressly argues that the 32-day PIP deviated from the bank’s 60-to-90-day policy without required documentation or approval, lacked required safeguards, and that the “unexplained compression” permits an inference of pretext/retaliatory cover story rather than a legitimate performance process.

criteria_results.title: Chronological timeline of key events presented
criteria_results.reasoning: The memorandum’s disputed facts section presents a chronological sequence including April 3 internal report, May 2 internal conclusion, July 28 OCC inquiry, August 1 Hargrove email, August 14 PIP, and September 22 termination. That is at least five of the seven specified events in chronological order.

criteria_results.title: ISSUE_004: Temporal proximity argued as supporting causation
criteria_results.reasoning: The memorandum expressly argues that the OCC request and Hargrove's August 1 identification of Vasquez as the likely source were followed 13 days later by Caldwell issuing her first PIP, and states that this temporal sequence supports an inference that the disclosure contributed to the PIP and termination. It invokes close timing as causation evidence multiple times.

criteria_results.title: ISSUE_004: 99 days between FinCEN report and termination noted
criteria_results.reasoning: The memorandum states that the claim involved the “June 15 FinCEN report” and separately states that “Vasquez was terminated September 22.” These dates make the 99-day interval calculable, even though the memo does not expressly say “99 days.”

criteria_results.title: ISSUE_005: Comparative treatment of Whitfield and/or Lomax cited
criteria_results.reasoning: The memorandum expressly argues that two other SVPs under Caldwell, Whitfield and Lomax, received 'Needs Improvement' ratings but were not placed on PIPs, contrasting this with Vasquez’s recent 'Outstanding' review and using it as evidence of selective enforcement/pretext.

criteria_results.title: ISSUE_005: Whitfield's role in onboarding Orion Gateway highlighted
criteria_results.reasoning: The memorandum expressly states in the comparator/pretext discussion that Whitfield, another SVP, originated the Orion Gateway relationship, that Caldwell knew Whitfield was the relationship manager, and that Caldwell identified no discipline for him. This links Whitfield to the Orion Gateway entity at the center of the AML concerns and uses it to support disparate treatment of Vasquez.

criteria_results.title: ISSUE_006: Carlos Medina's declaration cited as corroboration
criteria_results.reasoning: The memorandum cites Carlos Medina's declaration multiple times to corroborate Vasquez's claims, including that Medina found layering indicators and recommended immediate SARs, that he was told to “stand down,” and that he was terminated shortly after Vasquez.

criteria_results.title: ISSUE_006: Medina's termination argued as pattern of retaliation
criteria_results.reasoning: The memorandum discusses Medina’s October 14 termination, the claimed restructuring, that he was the only employee removed, and that a substantially similar AML position was refilled about three weeks later. It also ties this evidence to the Bank’s response to internal reporting and pretext, reinforcing the retaliation inference. Although it does not name Rachel Gunther or use the exact phrase “broader pattern of retaliation,” it connects Medina’s termination to a pattern/context of retaliation against Orion Gateway-related internal reporting.

criteria_results.title: ISSUE_007: SOX subsidiary coverage argument made
criteria_results.reasoning: The memorandum expressly argues that Defendant's SOX coverage argument is legally incorrect because § 1514A covers subsidiaries whose financial information is included in a publicly traded parent's consolidated financial statements, and it identifies Ridgeline National Bank as a wholly owned subsidiary of NASDAQ-listed Ridgeline Financial Group, Inc. Although it does not mention the ticker symbol RDFG, the required subsidiary-coverage argument is clearly made.

criteria_results.title: ISSUE_007: Lawson v. FMR LLC or statutory text cited for SOX subsidiary coverage
criteria_results.reasoning: The memorandum expressly cites the text of 18 U.S.C. § 1514A(a), including the subsidiary/affiliate language for consolidated financial statements, and also cites Lawson v. FMR LLC in support of SOX coverage extending beyond publicly traded entities. This satisfies the criterion.

criteria_results.title: ISSUE_008: Federal preemption argument rebutted for state law claim
criteria_results.reasoning: The memorandum expressly rebuts preemption of the Colorado public-policy wrongful termination claim, arguing there is no field or conflict preemption, that the BSA contains no textual basis for occupying the field, and that the state tort complements federal whistleblower protections by deterring retaliation and encouraging reporting. It also notes overlapping remedies are not an obstacle to federal schemes.

criteria_results.title: ISSUE_008: Absence of express preemption language noted
criteria_results.reasoning: The memorandum argues that the BSA lacks textual support for preemption and states generally that no federal statute/neither statute preempts the Colorado claim, but it does not specifically note or argue that SOX contains no express preemption language displacing state-law claims. The criterion requires the specific point as to both BSA and SOX.

criteria_results.title: ISSUE_009: Inadequacy of internal investigation argued
criteria_results.reasoning: The memorandum expressly states that Hargrove declared the Orion Gateway matter “reviewed and resolved” on May 2 before Medina completed his work, that Prescott had no written analysis supporting that conclusion, and that the review was shorter than expected. It also characterizes the Bank’s conduct as suppressing a compliance investigation and declining required reporting, using those facts in support of retaliatory/pretext arguments. This satisfies the criterion.

criteria_results.title: ISSUE_009: Dr. Redmond's expert opinion on investigation adequacy cited
criteria_results.reasoning: The memorandum cites Redmond only for identifying AML red flags and opining that the activity warranted reporting; it does not cite Dr. Redmond's expert opinion that the bank's internal investigation was facially inadequate or otherwise reference her opinion on investigation inadequacy.

criteria_results.title: ISSUE_009: Sham investigation linked to retaliation inference
criteria_results.reasoning: The memorandum discusses the AML investigation's inadequacy—Hargrove prematurely deemed the matter resolved, Medina was told to stand down, and there was no written analysis—and it even references a decision to suppress the compliance investigation. But it does not clearly use that sham or inadequate investigation as a causation/pretext argument that the Bank wanted to suppress Vasquez’s concerns rather than address them and therefore terminated her in retaliation. The retaliation inference is primarily tied to source-hunting, timing, PIP irregularities, and performance pretext, not the inadequate investigation itself.

criteria_results.title: ISSUE_010: Caldwell's inability to explain $15M target highlighted
criteria_results.reasoning: The memorandum expressly highlights the $10M written target versus the $15M PIP target, cites Caldwell Dep. 34–38, states Caldwell could not identify when the increase was communicated and knew of no written amendment, and argues a jury could view the retroactive $15M target as fabricated or selectively invoked. Although it does not use the exact quoted phrases 'believed' or 'recall the specifics,' it substantively highlights Caldwell's inability to substantiate the $15M target and ties it to post hoc fabrication.

criteria_results.title: ISSUE_011: Credibility determinations inappropriate at summary judgment
criteria_results.reasoning: The memorandum expressly invokes the Rule 56 principle that the court must not weigh evidence, resolve conflicts, or make credibility determinations, and repeatedly argues that disputes over Caldwell/Hargrove's explanations, timing, and pretext are for the jury rather than summary judgment.

criteria_results.title: ISSUE_011: Anderson v. Liberty Lobby or Reeves v. Sanderson cited
criteria_results.reasoning: The memorandum cites Anderson v. Liberty Lobby in the summary-judgment standard for the principle that the court may not weigh evidence or make credibility determinations, and also cites Reeves in connection with pretext and impermissible credibility determinations at summary judgment.

criteria_results.title: Prima facie case for BSA retaliation (31 U.S.C. § 5328) constructed
criteria_results.reasoning: The memorandum expressly constructs the BSA retaliation case: it identifies protected activity under § 5328 through Vasquez's April 3 internal AML/SAR memorandum and June 15 FinCEN report; explains that the employer knew of the internal report and at least suspected she triggered the regulatory inquiry; identifies adverse actions including the PIP and termination; and develops causation through the August 1 email, close timing, decisionmaker involvement, and pretext evidence. Thus the prima facie elements are articulated.

criteria_results.title: Prima facie case for SOX retaliation (18 U.S.C. § 1514A) constructed
criteria_results.reasoning: The memorandum articulates and applies the SOX contributing-factor framework, discusses protected disclosures/activities, employer and decisionmaker knowledge, adverse actions including PIP and termination, and causal connection through timing, source-identification evidence, and pretext. Although the SOX section emphasizes coverage and incorporates earlier factual arguments rather than listing elements in a standalone checklist, it sufficiently constructs a prima facie SOX retaliation case.

criteria_results.title: Prima facie case for Colorado wrongful termination constructed
criteria_results.reasoning: The memorandum expressly addresses the Colorado public-policy wrongful discharge claim, cites Colorado authority, identifies the relevant elements, and applies them by arguing that BSA/AML reporting of suspicious transactions is protected by a clear public policy and that Vasquez was terminated for engaging in that reporting. This constructs the required prima facie case.
